title: 5 Questions With Memphis Mainstay Willie Gregory
summary: The man called the “unofficial mayor of Memphis” talks about giving back to the city that shaped him, creating opportunities for the next generation, and carrying Memphis‘ legacy forward.
body_markdown:
From its singular pork ribs and fried catfish to the wailing, rhythmic riffs of rock ‘n’ roll and the blues, Memphis has helped birth American cultural identity and ingenuity.


But it’s also known as the place of an ending. Blocks from bustling Beale Street, on April 4, 1968, a bullet dashed one of our country’s greatest dreamers, a Southern preacher whose words galvanized the world.


Willie Gregory, Nike Senior Director, Community Relations, was a teenager living in Memphis on that fateful evening. The moment changed him. Inside, it sparked something.


In the nearly 60 years since Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. died on a motel balcony near Gregory’s old neighborhood, Gregory has firmly planted roots in the city, on a mission to reshape its narrative.


He has served Nike for more than 30 years from here, working with others to create opportunities for employment and education while developing a reputation as the “unofficial mayor” of Memphis. From sitting on the board of trustees for city museums to serving on the city’s chamber of commerce to his role in bringing the University of Memphis athletics into the Nike family, Gregory’s impact has been immense.


There is so much life in Memphis, Gregory says. It’s important to him that people feel that sense of energy and community while also honoring the past. Which is why he and his Memphis teammates helped launch[the Nike Kids 3K](https://about.nike.com/en/mission/initiatives/community-engagement) , a late-summer race that begins and ends outside the Lorraine Motel, where Dr. King was killed.


The building has since been reimagined as the[National Civil Rights Museum](https://civilrightsmuseum.org/) , dedicated to telling the story about the injustice Dr. King battled and how that fight has evolved in the years since his death. Today, the museum also serves as a key access point to movement and teamwork for children in the region thanks in part to the efforts of Gregory, who served on the museum’s board of directors from 2002 to 2015.


Gregory joined us recently for a walk to the museum to discuss his city, his mission at Nike and how the company is helping him give back to a community that means so much to him.
